Definitions:
- MOTTE_BAILEY: a speaker makes Claim A; another person challenges it (Challenge C); the ORIGINAL speaker replies with Claim B that retreats to a narrower, weaker or more easily defensible position while presenting it as if it still defends Claim A.
- STRAWMAN: one person makes Claim A; a DIFFERENT person replies with Claim B that misrepresents Claim A as a different, stronger or more extreme position and argues against that distorted version.
- NONE: no such move - an honest clarification, an open concession, a fair paraphrase, a genuine question, or ordinary disagreement with what was actually said.

Here is a motte-and-bailey-shaped (A, challenge C, then the same speaker's reply B) example taken from a real online discussion, with its human label:

Claim A: The public needs to know a company is becoming an abusive monopoly before it happens, and without government involvement there's no obligation to inform people; also, what if a company only turns abusive after already gaining monopoly power?
Challenge C: Competitors and journalists already have an incentive to expose abusive companies (and already do); government can lie too; an abusive monopoly creates demand for alternatives, which undermines itself.
Claim B: I'm not saying that's wrong, but the free-market promise that information + rational spending fixes everything rarely holds in practice -- even when info leaks (e.g. child-labor chocolate) it often has no effect, especially when the monopoly itself blocks new competition from forming (e.g. owning the only cable lines).
Label: MOTTE_BAILEY

Write exactly 2 new examples and return them as JSON:
{"variants": [{"kind": "...", "claim_A": "...", "challenge": "...", "claim_B": "...", "label": "..."}]}

Variant 1, kind "paraphrase": the SAME exchange reworded with different words and sentence structure, same meaning, same rhetorical move. label: MOTTE_BAILEY.
Variant 2, kind "topic_transfer": a DIFFERENT everyday debate topic with the SAME logical move as the original. label: MOTTE_BAILEY.

Style: informal, like real Reddit comments; similar length to the original; 1-3 sentences per claim. Ignore bracketed editorial notes such as "[Content note: ...]" and do not copy them. Never name the fallacy in the text. Every variant needs a non-empty challenge.

variants.claim_A: People deserve a heads-up that a company is turning into an abusive monopoly before it's too late, and if the government isn't involved nobody's required to tell them anything. Plus, what happens when a company only goes bad after it already has monopoly power?
variants.challenge: Rivals and reporters already have every reason to call out abusive companies, and they do it all the time. Governments can lie too, and a company that abuses its monopoly creates demand for alternatives, so it sort of sinks itself.
variants.claim_B: I'm not saying you're wrong there, but the idea that more info plus rational buyers solves everything almost never works out in real life. Even when stuff gets out, like the child-labor chocolate thing, it usually changes nothing, especially if the monopoly is what stops competitors from showing up, like owning the only cable lines.
variants.label: MOTTE_BAILEY

variants.claim_A: Landlords should have to disclose a building's mold problems before anyone signs a lease, and without city inspections there's no reason they'd ever tell tenants. Also, what if the mold only shows up after people have already moved in?
variants.challenge: Tenants already post reviews and local news outlets cover bad landlords all the time. City inspectors can be bribed or lazy too, and a landlord with a moldy building ends up with vacancies, so the market punishes them anyway.
variants.claim_B: I'm not saying that's wrong, but the idea that reviews and informed renters fix everything rarely works in practice. Even when the info is out there, like those well-known slumlord buildings that stay full, people often have no effect on them, especially in tight housing markets where renters can't afford to walk away.
variants.label: MOTTE_BAILEY
